newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia eyes big fuel oil exports but doubts abound.
newsitem.headline: Russia eyes big fuel oil exports but doubts abound.

text.p: Russia hopes to export fuel oil aggressively to the West this year during the peak summer season, but weak prices and high transport costs could limit volumes, fuel oil traders said on Thursday.
But some traders doubted exports between June and November would be particularly high, citing quality problems and low prices.

"I am still looking for around 5.5 million tonnes of fuel oil through Russia's northern ports between May and November this year," said one trader based in the main northern oil and products outlet of St Petersburg.
He said 4.5 million tonnes of Russian fuel oil, also known as mazut, would move through St Peterburg itself, with another one million tonnes coming through Arkhangelsk and Kandalaksha.
Early expectations pointed to a roughly even split between M-40 and M-100 grades.
A second trader specialising in Baltic Sea exports said mazut deliveries from Ventspils and Klaipeda were likely to be strong this summer, reaching 500,000 to 600,000 tonnes a month.
"Business is brisk at the moment," he said. "Combined fuel oil exports through Ventspils, Klaipeda and Tallinn could well be in excess of half a million tonnes a month this summer."
The outlook for exports through the Mediterranean was less positive, one Black Sea fuel oil trader said, but he would not give a forecast for monthly shipments.
"Prices are low in the Med and it is proving a problem for some mazut producers," he said. "This will impact volumes, but some Russian material will continue to flow to the Black Sea."
If the more bullish mazut exports were fulfilled, Russia could export up to 1.34 million tonnes of fuel oil per month through ports in northern Russia and the Baltics.

And based on the assumption that Black Sea exports account for around a quarter of Russia's exports through western ports, total monthly summer exports could hit 1.80 million tonnes, and comfortably above 10 million tonnes for the six-month season.

Russian refineries produced over 60 million tonnes of fuel oil in 1996, by far the most important single product by volume. Many of the biggest plants want to reduce mazut output and turn out lighter, more valuable products.

But the shift away from heavy fuel oil, used mainly in power stations and fuel for ships, is likely to be a slow one, because Russian oil firms are struggling to raise hundreds of millions of dollars needed to upgrade refineries.
Russia is the key mazut supplier to Western Europe, and shipments continue throughout the year through Black Sea ports.
The Baltic shipping route to Rotterdam closes every winter due to freezing waters, and a flood of exports hit the markets around May of each year, when waters thaw.
Several traders questioned Russia's ability to export huge volumes this year, saying that prices were already weak in Europe even before the full impact of the summer flood was felt.

"I don't think we will have anywhere near that amount. My experience of the last three to four years has told me that four million tonnes really means two to 2.5 million tonnes," said one London-based Russian fuel oil dealer.
"I think exports will be no more than 3.0-3.5 million from St Petersburg and 5.0-5.5 million tonnes including Ventspils and other northern and Baltic outlets this summer," he added.
The trader said some Russian fuel oil would fail to meet quality requirements in the West, while high domestic rail transportation costs would also limit shipments.
The bulk of Russia's fuel oil moves from refineries, often located thousands of kilometres from the ports, in rail wagons.
If high-sulphur fuel oil cargoes cif northwest Europe fell much below $80 a tonne, Russian refineries may well start to limit exports, the London trader said.
A Moscow-based dealer agreed that mazut exports were likely to be hampered by high rail costs.
"If rail costs remain at this level, then to expect exports of much more than five million tonnes from Russia during the summer would be asking a lot," he said.

First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, in charge of re-vamping Russia's natural monopolies including the railways, has said he intended to lower rail tariffs later this year. But such a move may not come soon enough for the 1997 summer season.

One trader said another problem for Russian fuel oil exporters were high shipping costs, with chartering rates for northwest European fuel oil tankers already on the rise in response to increased demand from Russia.

Most traders agreed the economics of exporting fuel oil to Europe were difficult, but some said cash-strapped refineries and traders would continue to export aggressively to earn much-needed hard currency.
